claims.text: Rapid-solidification processing produces a more refined grain structure than conventional casting in lightweight high-entropy alloys.
Rapid-solidification processing produces a more uniform microstructure than conventional casting.
The refined and uniform microstructure produced by rapid solidification improves mechanical strength.
The refined and uniform microstructure produced by rapid solidification improves corrosion resistance.
The refined and uniform microstructure produced by rapid solidification improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Rapid-solidification processing preserves the alloy's low density relative to conventional casting.
Rapid solidification generates a homogeneous distribution of nanoscale second phases.
Refined grains and homogeneously distributed nanoscale second phases facilitate formation of a stable, protective oxide layer.
Rapid solidification suppresses phase segregation.
Rapid solidification limits grain coarsening.
The resulting refined grain structure enhances strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
The resulting microstructure produces a uniform, adherent surface oxide layer.
A uniform, adherent oxide layer protects the alloy against corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
Relative to the cast baseline, the rapidly solidified alloy will have statistically significantly higher tensile strength.
Relative to the cast baseline, the rapidly solidified alloy will have a lower corrosion rate.
Relative to the cast baseline, the rapidly solidified alloy will show lower oxidation mass gain over time.
Excessive porosity or inclusions introduced by rapid-solidification processing can negate the benefits of microstructural refinement.
Extremely aggressive corrosive media or sufficiently high temperatures can exceed the protective capability of the oxide layer.
The link between rapid solidification and microstructural refinement is well established.
The magnitude of property improvements depends on processing parameters and alloy composition.
